description: We are a multidisciplinary team of Electrical, Mechanical, Mechatronics, and Artificial Intelligence students passionate about aerospace engineering, robotics, and emerging technologies. Our mission is to combine engineering expertise, AI, and software development to build an innovative, interactive astronaut mission simulator. We aim to create a technically ambitious, scientifically grounded project. We welcome creative problem-solvers with skills in programming, game design, and space science.
summary:
Moonbase Academy is an offline iPhone and iPad game for children ages 7–12 that turns a lunar outpost into a repeatable science experiment. Players choose equipment and operating settings, predict an outcome, explain their reasoning, test the plan and use evidence to revise a decision.

Four drills explore power, life support, food production, storm sheltering and communication delay. Choices have costs: another empty battery cannot create energy, while reducing air-maker power saves electricity but consumes stored oxygen. Ready-to-use example labs let reviewers explore these trade-offs without unlocking buildings or changing a saved base.

NASA crew-resource references, Veggie information, archived solar-particle-event timestamps and the average Earth–Moon distance inform the model. Reference data, derived calculations and simplified training rules are identified separately. The working native prototype aims to help young learners explain why a mission succeeds or fails, with offline play and opportunities to try another strategy.
details:
Moonbase Academy turns a lunar outpost into a repeatable engineering experiment for children ages 7–12. Players choose equipment and operating settings, predict an outcome, explain their reasoning, observe a simulation and revise their plan using evidence.

The central lesson is that every decision has consequences. In the starter Shadow lab, one solar array and one battery store 2.4 kWh during sunlight, while the six-hour shadow requires 3.6 kWh at Full air. Power runs out at mission hour 10. Keeping the equipment unchanged and reducing only shadow air-maker power to Half completes the 12-hour mission. This saves 1.5 kWh while consuming approximately 0.2 kg of stored oxygen. Adding an empty battery alone cannot solve insufficient energy generation.

Four drills explore power and life support, a 33-day food-production budget, sheltering during archived solar storms, and Earth–Moon communication delay. Own-base experiments connect the player's working equipment to the simulation. Ready-to-use Shadow and Storm labs allow experimentation without unlocking buildings or changing saved campaign progress.

NASA information meaningfully affects outcomes. BVAD references inform adult crew oxygen and food consumption. Veggie information informs the crop period and garden-power reference. CCMC archived particle-event timestamps determine storm rehearsal durations. NASA's average Earth–Moon distance and the SI speed of light determine radio delay and rover stopping behavior.

Reference values, derived calculations, physical constants and authored training assumptions are identified separately. Equipment capacities, simplified air-maker behavior and the six-hour shadow are teaching rules. Archived storms are not live forecasts, and the app does not calculate lunar radiation dose.

The native offline prototype uses Swift, SwiftUI, SpriteKit, Core Graphics, Foundation and XCTest. It requires no account or backend. The latest verification includes 154 unit tests and three selected simulator UI tests with passing latest results. These checks establish technical behavior; no child learning-effectiveness study is claimed.

The intended benefit is accessible exploration at home or in classrooms: make a prediction, change one variable and explain why the result changed. Further work includes learner testing and accessibility refinement.
